abstract: Fang et al. conduct a large-scale experiment to measure how AI writing assistance distorts the perceived personas of writers across political beliefs, personality traits, and demographic identity. In the study, 2,939 writers composed political opinion paragraphs both with and without AI assistance, while 11,091 readers evaluated 10,008 paragraphs across 29 socially salient perception dimensions, generating 2,903,596 total ratings. The results show that AI writing assistance produced persona distortions across all measured dimensions: writers appeared more opinionated, more competent, and more positive when using AI tools, and their perceived demographic profiles shifted toward more privileged groups. This homogenization effect flattens persona distinctiveness, making AI-assisted writers sound more alike regardless of their actual backgrounds, beliefs, or writing styles. Critically, writers objected to many of these distortions when made aware of them, yet still preferred AI-assisted text over their unassisted writing — revealing a tension between authenticity and perceived quality. The authors developed mitigation strategies using reward models trained on experimental data to steer AI outputs toward more faithful writer representation, but found an entanglement between desirable properties (fluency, persuasiveness) and undesirable distortions (persona flattening, demographic shifting), making full resolution difficult.
keyFindings: AI writing assistance produced measurable persona distortions across all 29 perception dimensions tested
Writers using AI appeared more opinionated, competent, and positive, with demographic profiles shifting toward more privileged groups
Writers objected to persona distortions when made aware but still preferred AI-assisted text over unassisted writing
Reward-model-based mitigation reduced objectionable distortions but decreased user acceptance, revealing trade-offs between authenticity and quality
Homogenization effect flattens individual distinctiveness — AI-assisted writers sound increasingly alike regardless of background
methodology: Large-scale randomized experiment with 2,939 writers and 11,091 readers. Writers composed political opinion paragraphs with and without AI assistance. Blind reader evaluations across 29 socially salient perception dimensions (political opinion, writing quality, personality, emotions, demographics). 10,008 paragraphs analyzed with 2,903,596 total ratings. Mitigation tested via reward models trained on experimental data.
qualifiers: Limited to political opinion writing — distortion patterns may differ for other genres or professional contexts. English-language only. Perception dimensions are reader-assessed proxies, not ground truth. The entanglement between quality improvement and persona distortion suggests this is a fundamental challenge, not merely a tuning problem. Does not measure downstream labor market effects of writing homogenization.
